newsitem.title: USA: Arizona's sticky cotton problem finally unglued?.
newsitem.headline: Arizona's sticky cotton problem finally unglued?.

text.p: Arizona's sticky cotton problem could well disappear into the history books this year according to results obtained by the state's Cotton Research and Protection Council (ACRPC).
Thanks to two chemicals previously used successfully in Israel, the 1996 Arizona cotton crop is 99 percent sticky free, the council added in a statement.
This was defined as 98 percent graded zero or one - the latter being light stickiness. A further one percent was grade two which the ACRPC said generally did not affect the spinning process.
Last year 79 percent of the crop was graded zero and one, with a further 11 percent grade two, and 10 percent heavy stickiness.

"That's a very welcome change for Arizona's beleaguered cotton industry," said Larry Antilla, ACRPC staff director. "Since 1991, Arizona cotton has unfairly gained a sticky cotton reputation, resulting in hefty discounts of as much as eight cents per pound."
Sticky cotton, caused by bodywaste residues from whiteflies, cotton aphids and other insects, causes normally fluffy cotton fibers to become sticky.
Sticky cotton is shunned by many textile mills due to the difficulty in handling and spinning, the ACRPC said.

The two chemicals used, Applaud and Knack, were granted a one year Section 18 Environmental Protection Agency exemption due to difficulty in controlling whiteflies with synthetic pyrethroid chemistries, the ACRPC statement said.
To avoid resistance to the new chemicals, Arizona cotton growers will only use each chemical only once during the season.
